I wish also to express my approval of what the hon. member for Hastings-Peterborough (Mr. White) said on this subject, and incidentally the point which the hon. member for York-Sunbury (Mr. Hanson) made a moment ago is one that needed to be dealt with. I could never understand the position that has been taken heretofore in regard to that matter. I may also say that I am heartily in accord with the wisdom of creating a separate department of veterans' affairs. I know this has been urged by the various veterans' associations and I am glad that the government has now agreed to bring in a bill to set up a separate veterans affairs' department. These veterans have earned our undying gratitude, and it is our simple duty to do everything we can to ensure that when they return they will find that their opportunities for rehabilitation have been well taken care of by those of us who have benefited from their services and who have remained in security at home. Not only that, but I think we should make sure that the dependents of those soldiers are given the most generous treatment that it is possible to give them.
With regard to this bill to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs I should like to emphasize the importance of a man, before being discharged or demobilized, having a complete medical examination and that the examining board should decide at that time the question of eligibility for pension. This would have the effect of sending men to this department who otherwise might feel, as happened after the last war, that their chances of pension were too slight to be pursued. While this may be true at the moment of discharge it is highly important that a complete medical history be on record in the department, so that if there is a subsequent deterioration in the veteran's health this will form a basis for a later pension claim. I am informed that at the present time many discharged men are not given any definite instructions about their rights with respect to pensions.

I was so informed, but I am glad if it is not the case.
The present practice of discharging men while undergoing active hospital treatment is so inhuman that it should be discontinued forthwith. A man should be kept on the strength during the whole of his initial hospital treatment. Of course this will mean that in a few cases men who will spend the rest of their lives in hospitals will be considered members of the active forces until their death. This I believe will have a decided moral value, while entailing very little additional expense.
The setting up of this department will in my judgment ensure that veterans will receive better consideration than has been the case heretofore. At present their interests are divided among a number of departments. This offers too many opportunities for passing the buck. My veteran friends know what that means. By having one minister responsible for all the interests of veterans, which would include directing them to suitable hospitals for medical care, they will undoubtedly receive more consideration than under the present situation.
In passing I may say, since I have not taken advantage of the opportunity to say it before, that I consider the clothing allowance of 865 on discharge to be quite- insufficient, and I think this should at least be doubled.
The rehabilitation grant of one month's pay and allowances is also quite inadequate to bridge the gap between discharge and the resumption of civilian employment. This gap is bound to be governed to a great extent by the length of service, since a man who lias lived for three or four years under army routine will not adapt himself quickly to civilian life. I do not think the rehabilitation grant should be considered in any sense a reward for service; it should merely be designed to effect, as soon as possible, its avowed purpose of reestablishment.
The provisional routine order No. 1079 which debars men discharged at their own request, or members of the permanent force, from receiving rehabilitation grants, should be washed out, because this class, more than most others, require this grant.
On March 20, the Prime Minister moved two resolutions which had the effect of setting
100-241*
up two separate ministries to replace the present Department of Pensions and National Health. The first of these measures is bill No. S3, which we are considering to-day, to establish a Department of Veterans' Affairs. The bill which will set up the other division, namely, the Department of Social Welfare, has not yet been brought down.
In the process of expanding the Department of Pensions and National Health into two departments, under separate ministries, unfortunately the word "'health" disappeared. This,
I venture to say, is a mistake. After all, the promotion of good health is the most important function that any social service could render. The Department of Veterans' Affairs will be responsible for care and treatment, and training for reestablishment in civil life as it affects members of the armed forces.
I think it might be well at this time to give the committee the opinion of the Canadian Medical association, which gave careful consideration to this whole matter at its recent 75th annual meeting in Toronto, and which sent to the Prime Minister on May 29 certain observations, of which I have a copy and which, for the information of the house, I should like to read into the record. I should say in passing that this organization represents a great majority of the medical profession in Canada, and has been in close touch with all recent developments in the provision of health services. It has had five of its members sitting on the Canadian medical procurement and assignment board, which was established by order in council in July, 1942.
The Canadian Medical Association desires to make the following observations:
1.	Following upon the organization of the Department of Soldier reestablishment in 1919 the present Department of Pensions and National Health was established in 1928, after much discussion and many representations made to the government by groups and individuals concerned not only in problems relating to the care of veterans, but also with the wider conception of a national health policy, in respect of all health matters _ properly falling within the scope of national jurisdiction.
2.	The proposal to set up in Canada for the first time such a department was warmly welcomed throughout the country and regarded as a procedure of national importance.
3.	In the present resolutions the provision for a department of health under that name, either alone or in combination with other similar interests, does not appear.
4.	If a directorate dealing .with national health is to be retained, it would appear that it would be one of several departments within the proposed new Department of Social Welfare.
5.	If eventually a plan for health insurance be devised requiring federal assistance and a
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

degree of federal oversight and guidance it will presumably -be administered within the new Department of Social Welfare.
6.	Inasmuch as the health of the people depends to a great extent upon the environmental conditions under which they live and work, upon security against fear and want, upon adequate nutrition, and upon their opportunities for exercise and leisure, as well as upon a health service which will ensure that everybody in the country irrespective of means, age, sex or occupation shall have an equal opportunity to benefit from the best and most up-to-date medical and allied services available, the term national health, in its modern implications, appears to be broad enough to include most, if not all of the functions of the proposed Department of Social Welfare.
7.	Abundant evidence supports the view that the nation is more conscious than ever before of the importance and scope of developments which are anticipated within the health field, and that it is desirable to emphasize in all reasonable ways the importance of the health programme.
8.	For the reasons cited, and having regard only to the best interests of the Canadian people, we would respectfully suggest that -the new department for which the name of social welfare is now proposed might well be called the department of national health.
9.	As we understand the present proposals, the medical and hospital care of veterans and their dependents as now carried on in the Department of Pensions and National Health would be transferred to the new Department of Veterans' Affairs.
10.	A great national plan for health care is being devised, and it may be assumed that when and if it comes into operation a large number of our people, consisting of the veterans who with their dependents, will constitute 12 to 15 per cent of our population, might reasonably expect to have access to these services.
11.	Again most respectfully we would urge that in the interests of sound administration, careful consideration be given to placing all government health services in time of peace within one department.
12.	In order to concentrate the expenditure for veterans' care w'ithin one department, the Department of Veterans Affairs could arrange to purchase the "medical care"-using the term broadly-for this group of people from the department of national health.
13.	We believe that if the health services were so organized, there would be a notable conservation of medical and technical personnel and equipment and that there would be provided a finer type of service to this very-important group.
14.	Summarizing we would most respectfully suggest:
(a)	That the title "department of national health" is preferable to "department of social welfare."
(b)	That all federal health activities be incorporated in the department of national health, including the health and care of veterans.
All of which is respectfully submitted on behalf of the Canadian medical association.
T. C. Routley,
Secretary.
I should like now to give a brief outline of the qualifications of this association to indicate that their opinions are deserving of respect and careful consideration. May I recall that the primary function of the medical procurement and assignment board was to secure physicians for the armed forces and at the same time to endeavour to preserve adequate medical services for the civilian population. As time went on, it became apparent that the health services of the country as a whole required to be studied, and this involved physicians, dentists, nurses, medical schools, public health, medical research, industry and the community generally. The personnel of the board consisted of three directors of the medical services, army, navy and air force, a representative of the Department of Pensions and National Health, the medical director'of national war services and a representative or director of national selective service. There were also the director of the dental service and five members of the Canadian medical association advisory committee to which I referred a moment ago.
The scope of the character of the board's activities was widened to make possible a national survey which was completed in January, 1943. The report which they published about two months ago consists of ten parts and constitutes a fairly valuable compilation of the available civilian man-power, the war medical man-power, medical nurses, public health, hospital personnel and facilities, industrial medicine, nurses, dental services and concludes with certain recommendations. I am mentioning this to indicate the wide knowledge at the disposal of the Canadian Medical association when it made the proposals which I read a moment ago and which, therefore, I venture to suggest deserve careful consideration. Speaking for myself as a surgeon, I am entirely in accord with those proposals and I hope that when the new department is created it will be called the department of national health.
May I point out that at the present moment the social security committee has about completed the consideration of the national health insurance bill which, if enacted into law, will provide an all-inclusive health service for our people. There is no reason why our veterans should be excluded from the benefits which will be provided under that bill. The federal government will be called upon to pay a large sum of money annually to provide these services which will include additional hospital, diagnostic and treatment centres equipped with all modern facilities, as well as skilled specialists in all departments.
(Mr. Bruoe.]

Department of Veterans' Affairs
From the report which is available to members of the house it is made clear that we have not a sufficient number of these specialists at the present moment to go around and therefore we must conserve our available skill. I ask the minister to consider whether it would not be economically sounder as well as in the best interests of the veterans themselves to do as the Canadian Medical Association has suggested, rather than set up another hospital service for veterans in addition to that existing at the present time.
I should like to refer to the question I raised a week ago following an item in the Montreal Gazette in which Doctor Penfield, an internationally known neuro-surgeon, made certain statements which I did not then give but which I propose reading now. This statement made on May 30 appeared in the director's report presented at the annual meeting of the Montreal neurological institute, and it is as follows:
It had been suggested to the Department of Pensions and National Health, Doctor Penfield said, that if the government wished to use the institute as a treatment centre, an annex for the treatment of service patients should be constructed. The plan had been turned down, he added, and the official reason given was "fear of tile establishment of an embarrassing precedent."
"It is not for us to question this decision," Dr. Penfield continued, "but four and a half years of the war have now passed, and the Canadian government has done practically nothing to establish special centres for tile care of war injuries of the nervous system; nothing at all in Quebec and the maritimes."
"It seems possible that returning service men with wounds of nerves and spine and head may think little of embarrassing precedents, and much of their chance to regain their health."
Dr. Penfield declared that the institute should at once enlarge its bed capacity by rapidly building a permanent addition. This would depend, he said, on securing public support through McGill university, as well as the cooperation of the city of Montreal and the provincial government and from Ottawa "at least" construction priorities.
And again;
"In England there are twelve specialized neurosurgical hospital units in the emergency medical service system, and a head injuries hospital for army and air force in Oxford and other centres for the treatment of nerve injuries. The R.CA..M.C. has psychiatrists in large numbers to deal with functional disturbances in Canada, but strangely lacks provision to restore organic sufferers."
The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. Mackenzie), in reply to this, described Doctor Penfield's statement as unjustifiable and exceedingly inaccurate. He then stated the number of hospital beds that were available in Canada. I venture to say that in
giving the number of beds the minister disregarded entirely the point at issue. These general hospital beds had nothing to do with beds specially arranged or services especially provided for neurological surgery.
I put certain questions on the order paper and I have had some replies which are not sufficiently illuminating, so that I shall have to answer some of them myself.
I asked how many neurological institutes there were in Canada. As far as I know, there is only one surgical institute of that kind in this country, namely, the Montreal neurological institute, which was built largely by money donated by the Rockefeller foundation some years ago in order to provide a place in Canada where Doctor Penfield, an internationally known neuro-surgeon, could operate and carry on certain investigations into various diseases of the nervous system for which the Rockefeller committee considered him to be especially competent.
It is true that we have neuro-surgical work being done in a hospital in Toronto. I hesitate to mention its name. It is Christie street hospital. I may say that the work there is efficiently done by Doctor C. P. McCormick, who is an eminent neuro-surgical specialist. I think they have perhaps fifty beds there, and I am told that they could do with another fifty.
There is also a neurological centre at Vancouver, at Shaughnessy Heights, where Doctor I urnbull, who is also a skilled neuro-surgeon, does the work.
I have mentioned the only three places where this particular class of Work, I am informed, is being done in Canada at the present time. I think there should be another centre in Winnipeg so as to make it geographically easy for friends of patients to visit their relatives who are being taken care of in these institutions.
At present a distinguished neuro-surgeon, Brigadier Botterell is in England, in charge of the Canadian hospital at Basingstoke. He comes from Winnipeg and therefore, I think, would be available later on to carry on that work quite efficiently in Winnipeg when a centre is created there.
I also asked how many neuro-surgeons there are in Canada. I think I can answer that question. Besides Doctor Penfield in Montreal, there are Doctor Cone and Doctor Elvidge. In Toronto we have an able neurosurgeon, Doctor Kenneth Mackenzie in addition to Doctor C. P. McCormick. Then there is Doctor Turnbull in Vancouver and Doctor Botterell in Winnipeg when he returns from overseas. That makes seven. There may be one or two others whom I have neglected to
Department oj Veterans' Affairs

mention, who have perhaps undertaken this specialty recently. But I think that constitutes the entire number. The number engaged in this specialty is limited because of the limited field for such work, and therefore it is highly important that we make use of the services of these few skilled specialists to the full extent possible for our returned men.
I remember fifty years ago when I studied in London with Sir Victor Horsley, that he was about the only neuro-surgeon in England who was devoting himself to brain surgery. Later on, one of his pupils, Doctor Harvey Cushing, carried on this specialty first at Baltimore and subsequently in Boston, and at that time he was one of the first neuro-surgeons in America. The reason was partly due to the limited field, that no surgeon would care to devote himself exclusively to that work because he would probably not make a living. I mention this to indicate to the members of the house the great importance of using to the full, for the benefit of our returned men who will need them, the services of these men with special skill and the importance of spending anything that is necessary to provide them with easily accessible beds.
When Doctor Penfield offered the department space for an addition to the Montreal neurological institute I think the offer should have been jumped at, but. instead it was peremptorily turned down on the specious and totally unwarranted ground that other hospitals would ask for similar concessions. It is obvious that no hospitals in Canada other than those situated in the places I have indicated, close to medical schools where they have a specialist in this department of work, would be likely to ask for a similar concession. But if they did, I would grant them all the money necessary to provide that accommodation.
The committee of consultants of the three armed services, army, navy and air force, together with the Department of Pensions and National Health, began work about a month ago in regard to the establishment of special centres in Canada for the three most essential services-neuro-surgery, orthopaedics and plastic surgery. It was thought that these might be combined with advantage, perhaps with economy. Colonel R. I. Harris, of Toronto, an able surgeon, is chairman of that committee. I understand that Doctor Penfield and his associates, by an addition to the neurological institute, could take care of the work originating in St. Anne's and possibly for Quebec and the maritimes. What a pity that the department did not envisage years ago the kind Of cases for whom such centres would

be needed so that the buildings would now be completed and ready to receive patients who may be soon arriving. Another year or two must necessarily elapse before these centres can be ready, unless they are proceeded with more rapidly than the Sunnybrook Park hospital in Toronto.
In case any of my recent remarks should be considered prejudiced, I should like to quote from a paper which heretofore has not been unfriendly to this government-the Winnipeg Free Press. I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already referred to certain portions of this editorial. I do not intend to read it all, but there are two or three points which are worth recording. Speaking of the Deer Lodge hospital the writer states:
It was then urged that if more beds had to be provided they should be in a building placed as near as possible to the Manitoba Medical College, that is to say, near the General hospital which provides the clinical background for all the teaching of medicine in Manitoba.
With that statement I entirely agree.
The basic reason for this suggestion was that efficiency in the treatment of patients is greatly enhanced by there being available for them as high a concentration as possible of medical and surgical skill and knowledge. Good specialists are not and never will be plentiful. At the present time they are even scarcer than usual, largely because of the stubborn and ill-judged determination of the three defence departments each one to create and maintain their own medical service, with virtually no coordination between them. Hence the need always present and now acute to create new hospital facilities as near to existing key institutions in order to make available over as wide a circle of patients as possible the rare and delicate skills of the specialist.
The editorial goes on to refer to the reply of the minister in regard to the "embarrassment" of which I spoke a moment ago, and continues as follows:
Mr. Mackenzie proudly cited the large increase in the number of beds in hospitals operated by this department, but typically omitted any mention of what happens to the men who are put into the beds, which is the only point which interests Dr. Penfield. Mr. Mackenzie then had the nerve to remark that Dr. Penfield had displayed a remarkable lack of knowledge of the preparations that were being made to look after the service men. We venture the suggestion that Dr. Penfield knows more about them and of their efficiency than Mr. Mackenzie does and that it was this knowledge which made him speak out as he did. . . .
Hospitals, as we have said before, are not mere masses of bricks and mortar. They are concentrations of medical skill and knowledge. If they are not that they are nothing but shells and the patients in them suffer and die accordingly. Elsewhere in his annual' report, Dr. Penfield remarked that in the last analysis intimate cooperation in the treatment of disease

Department oj Veterans' Affairs
depended upon the proximity of pooled specialist skill. We recommend the wisdom of this remark to Mr. Mackenzie and his colleagues in the government.
I do not think I could have written a better
editorial myself, and I commend it to the attention of the. members of the house.

I view this bill as one which should receive careful consideration by every hon. member in the light of its importance to our rehabilitation plans. As I see it, the subject matter of this bill is the coordination ol the different bodies which have been handling veterans' affairs in the past, and it can mean either that we shall have an orderly transition back to civilian life of our service personnel, or chaos in the aftermath of the war. Upon the personnel of this particular department of government will largely depend which of the situations I have mentioned will develop.
On several occasions I have spoken in the house and placed on record the opinions of myself and the members of this group with respect to rehabilitation generally and the mechanics we shall have to employ if we are to achieve the social objectives for which we are fighting the war. In the time at my disposal this afternoon I am going to deal specifically with the bill itself; I shall not enter into all the ramifications of rehabilitation.
First, to my mind the bill is a step in the right direction, in that the government propose by it to concentrate under one department all the problems of the service personnel. I think that makes for more efficient administration and will guarantee to the service personnel the implementation of the regulations as written; because the real test of any legislation-at least that has been my
experience-is the administration, as to whether those whom the legislation is designed to help will receive the benefits provided, or otherwise. Now the bill does in my opinion change to some extent matters which in the past have been pretty well fixed. In the hands of the minister, under the terms of the bill, we are placing practically dictatorial powers. He has the privilege under the bill of determining contracts with institutions for the care of persons. He is permitted under section 6 on page 2 of the bill to make regulations, contracts and so forth. I am not quarrelling with that principle, but we shall have to be mindful of this fact. The present minister of pensions, with whose department I have had a great deal to do since becoming a member of the house, is an old soldier to the subject, knows the regulations, and in my experience has been sympathetic, and if at any time a problem is brought to his attention, as soon as he possibly can he sees that any matter complained of is rectified within the scope of the regulations. But when we are setting up a. system giving powers to a minister or any other individual we must be mindful of the fact that the competent and efficient minister who now heads the department may not be there in the aftermath of the war.

I am referring to paragraph (h) on page 3. In that section of the bill tip reference to the merchant navy is made; it is completely omitted. It makes provision for the government to deal with governments outside of Canada for services rendered in the army, the navy, or the air force, providing medical benefits, et cetera, but it completely omits any reference to the merchant navy. That particular branch of the service is one which in my opinion has been discriminated against right from the start of the war, while every member who has had cause to refer to them has pointed out that were it not for the services rendered by the merchant navy, with very little glory, without the benefit of uniform, or of the other attractive measures which the other services enjoy, the invasion of Europe to-day would not be possible. I suggest that in this clause the provisions now made for the other branches of the service should be extended to the merchant navy.
Again, at page 4, paragraph (i), which is a carry-over from page 3, there are words which I fail to understand, and I do not think that at this time they have any right to appear in a bill which is being presented to the Canadian House of Commons. Let me read these words:
. . . for the provision of measures of unemployment relief to former members of such forces and their dependents.
In reading that section of the bill I anticipate, and anyone will who reads it, that under the regulations to be administered by this department of government provision is being made for unemployment relief for members of service personnel fighting at the present time in Italy and in France. I cannot understand why those words should be there. Under the terms of the government's rehabilitation proposals, as contained in many documents, they have set out a programme that looks attractive on paper.

I have a copy of it here but I will not take up the time of the house reading it-is that we disagreed completely with the principle of using canteen funds for the purpose of paying unemployment relief to any member of the services serving in the present war. Is it? A member is at a disadvantage in discussing this bill because (he minister did not open the debate with a statement. I think that the minister should have made a statement before any debate took place. The hon. member for Vancouver North gave a very good analysis of the department of veterans' affairs. He mentioned several principles that should be kept in mind, in my opinion. When the department of veterans' affairs is set up I hope that the government will not completely uproot all of the personnel now handling war veterans' allowances, the Pensions Act, national health problems, the treatment branch of pensions and national health, and so on. It may be the desire, for reasons other than efficiency, of people who I have heard discuss the problem to lead the returning personnel to believe that all jobs connected with the department of veterans' affairs are to be reserved for and allocated to personnel serving in this war. Yet I feel that while they are entitled to representation on every bhard that has to do with the handling of their problems, so that the point of view of men serving in this *war may be understood, there are hundreds of service personnel from the last war, men who have already fought a war and won it for this country regardless of the fact that someone stole the peace, who are now serving on boards administering the different measures that I have indicated. They

Department o/ Veterans' Affairs
are efficient; they know the problems, and they know the machinery. I hope it is not the intention of the government to weed out the people now serving in that capacity, because it would be a mistake to head up this department with brand new men and to lose the experience of men who have sat in, studied and administered these problems for the last twenty years. It may be that they have not administered them as we should have liked; nevertheless they have done a good administrative job within the scope of the regulations.
In dealing with the department my experience has been that the administration has not been wrong but that the regulations require expanding and correcting in many respects. I believe there is now more scope and latitude being given and we should be very careful not to throw out the hundreds of men whe are now employed in those capacities and who are at an age where they cannot go out and compete in the labour market. In our rush to try to promise jobs to everyone coming back from this war let us not forget the old soldier and the contribution he has made, both in the last war and in the subsequent period of peace. I think there is growing up in Canada *a tendency to disregard completely the obligation that the country owes to the old soldier who has already made his contribution.
I listened with interest to the remarks this afternoon of the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Fair). I wish to join with him in the plea that he made to the government on behalf of the soldier settlers of the last war who are now appealing to the government for the -wiping off of the financial obligation that they still have against their lands. I think that should be done. It was a distressing and depressing situation to find in Ottawa a few weeks ago a group of veterans from Saskatchewan and Alberta who pointed out that since the outbreak of this war some six hundred odd veterans a year have been dispossessed of the land on which they were placed after the last war.
As some encouragement to those coming back at this time, whom we expect to place on the land under a scheme similar to that of the last war, attention should be paid to the agitation that is being carried on across the country by veterans of the last war with respect to the obligations still standing against their homes and farms, and the request that those obligations should be cancelled. I think we all are more or less in agreement on that.
. The machinery that is to be set up in this new department to administer its activities will be very important. One of the most important parts of it will be the welfare department work in conjunction with the
selective service and unemployment insurance offices. I think they are totally understaffed at the present time, and the machinery is completely inadequate. I do not care how efficient the Ottawa machine is or who the personnel is, because we must remember that the soldier is not going to be settled in Ottawa when he comes back. He is going to be settled back in his own community; and if an efficient staff is to be appointed then we must have men who are sensible and who understand the regulations and the problems of the soldiers back in the communities. These are the men with whom the soldiers will have first contact, and they are the ones who are going to sell them the whole reconstruction programme of the government. If the minister intends to carry out the programme that has been outlined he should lose no time in establishing a welfare officer in each of the different communities. This should be done now, not after the war is over when we have wholesale demobilization. That welfare officer should be back talking to the boys when they come home. He should have some contact with national defence. He should be endeavouring to get from national defence and the different military districts a precis of the file of each soldier in the service from his community and should endeavour to determine the soldier's employment possibilities, what training he has received in the army, and how he can be routed into the economy of the province. Those files should be ready before general demobilization takes place. Then when the men start coming back they will meet someone who is efficient, who has contact with industry and is in a position to guide the men into vocational training and to disability pensions, if that is necessary, and to route them to some employment in the community. Unless that is done I certainly fear the.results of demobilization as affecting my own particular section.
